newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-UCB rallies, raising more eyebrows.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UCB rallies, raising more eyebrows.

text.p: Belgian drugs, fine chemicals and plastic films group UCB's shares astounded Brussel bourse traders on Thursday for the fourth day this week.
The stock failed to lead the league table of percentage gainers with a 1.9-percent rise on Thursday, but the rise has still come after Wednesday's 7.6-percent jump.
With almost 3,100 shares changing hands at a price of 148,500 francs ($4,000) each, UCB again led volume.

The stock has been scoring one record high after another, but as the rally rolls on, brokers and analysts can only grasp at the possible reasons behind the spectacular explosion that began in early June when the share was at 96,550 francs.
The buyer could be "an aggressive company represented in the market by a broker who is probably well-informed about the future financial strategy of (UCB)," an analyst said .
He said it was unlikely a fund or funds would be buying such volumes "at such an expensive price."
"There is no real economic reason to explain this extraordinary situation except the fact that the strong U.S. dollar is profitable for UCB," KB Securities analyst Jurgen Fryges said.

But firms may be interested in buying UCB to get Zyrtec, UCB's anti-allergy drug. Zyrtec has been selling in the U.S. since March 1996. Its sales are expected to reach $250 million this year. Sales in the second quarter, which is peak hayfever season, rose 94 percent to $70 million, UCB's U.S. marketing partner for Zyrtec, Pfizer, said on Tuesday.
"We know that Solvay is very interested in Zyrtec," Fryges said, referring to a rival Belgian group.
Solvay has said it wants to strengthen its pharmaceuticals division and incorporating UCB would result in relatively few overlaps with existing Solvay products, some analysts said.

But Solvay spokesman Paul Muys denied the company had its sights on UCB. "With all the mergers we have seen in the pharmaceutical world, it is normal that this subject comes up again. But I can only deny it 1,000 percent."
He said Solvay was happy with both companies, controlled separately by Belgium's Solvay family through several holding companies, "as they are."
Analysts said a buy would provide few synergies, or few gains from economies of scale.
Also, Solvay and UCB shareholders are mostly the same so, there was no reason for the firms to buy shares in the market. They could easily buy from each other without moving the share.
A broker also said UCB was unlikely buying its own shares "because the capital of the company is tightly-held."
Stable, closely-held holding companies own just less than 40 percent of UCB's share capital.
UCB's rally has lifted its market capitalisation to 216.5 billion francs, almost four times the level at 1995-end.
Solvay's share has been more volatile, up almost 1.4 percent since end-1995. Its market capitalisation is about 182 billion.
While UCB was seen as expensive relative to its sector and the Bel-20 index .BFX, Solvay has been an underperformer.
Based on 1997 price/earnings, UCB stands at about 39, almost four times the Bel-20. Solvay stands at 14.
Financially, UCB is in better shape. At end-1996 debt/equity and debt/assets ratios were 0.98 and 0.49, respectively. Comparable figures at Solvay were 1.68 and 0.62.
In recent years, UCB has consistently been cutting its debt.
Other potential buyers mentioned include Pfizer and Johnson & Johnson, both of the U.S.
Johnson & Johnson already owns Janssen Pharmaceutica, one of Belgium's other main drugs companies.
The U.S. firms could buy UCB relatively cheaply because of the dollar's strength against the Belgian franc, analysts said.
